sample.title: Why Sanctions Aren't Stopping North Korea
sample.description:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has raked in as much as $22 billion in foreign earnings from 2022 to 2025, according to a Bloomberg Economics analysis. That represents a 400% rise in revenues from the previous four-year period despite sweeping global sanctions. 

So how did Kim do it, and why is a richer North Korea an even bigger concern for the world?

sample.title: Who dominates hybrid car sales?
sample.description:
Just three automakers control the majority of one of the hottest segments in the U.S. car market — and none of them are American companies.

In the first half of 2026, sales of hybrid cars — not long ago considered a bridge to fully electric vehicles — have risen nearly 20% year-over-year to a record market share of 15.4%, according to the Center for Automotive Research, almost three times the share of pure EVs.

CNBC's Robert Ferris has the details.

Find the full report in related video.

sample.title: How SpaceX's AI ambitions took over Memphis
sample.description:
Two years after Elon Musk made Greater Memphis the center of his artificial intelligence ambitions, building data centers and energy infrastructure at breakneck speed, residents are grappling with unwanted effects, including noise and emissions from the natural gas-burning turbines. 

Now, public opposition to the SpaceXAI sites, known as Colossus and Colossus II, is providing a blueprint for other communities across the country opposed to AI developments.

sample.title: How High Diesel Prices Are Creating A Hidden Tax For Consumers
sample.description:
California is home to the busiest containership ports in the country. Many of the goods that enter through those ports must travel hundreds or even thousands of miles before they reach distribution centers, meaning a portion of the supply chain pays California diesel prices-the most expensive in the U.S. CNBC’s Pippa Stevens breaks down what that means for consumers.

Fifa boss Gianni Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged 'lover' | BBC News
sample.description:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino's alleged lover received a six-figure severance payment from Uefa while he was the organisation's general secretary, according to a Daily Telegraph investigation.
 
The Telegraph reported that the woman had an alleged relationship with Infantino, who is married, during his time at European football's governing body.
 
A spokesman for Infantino said he "strongly denies these categorically untrue allegations".
 
The claims come as Infantino fights for his future as Fifa president following his abandoned plans to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.
